## Paper

## Abstract

Ferroelectrics holds significant promise for a wide range of applications owing to their spontaneous polarization characteristics. Despite exhibiting multiple polarization mechanisms that demonstrate significant potential for electromagnetic functional materials, the practical deployment of ferroelectric polymers has been inhibited by the lack of precise control over polymer chains at the atomic scale and the relatively low stability of the polar phase. Here, a procedure of fortifying the ferroelectric polyvinylidene fluoride phase is proposed by the facet modulation, achieving stable ferroelectric polymer through engineering the interaction between the inorganic rigid crystal facets and organic flexible molecular chains at the atomic scale. The constructed polar ferroelectric polymers composite systems exhibit a broad distribution of relaxation times along with multi-polarization characteristics from megahertz to terahertz frequencies. The composite system mitigates the apparent loss-bandwidth trade-off, thereby achieving broadband polarization properties across multiple frequency bands while maintaining a dissipation efficiency above 99.9%. The demonstrated approach presents a breakthrough in achieving the stable ferroelectric polymers through facet-induced stabilization, providing deep insights for the development of high-performance electromagnetic functional materials.

---

## Introduction

Organic ferroelectric polymers demonstrate considerable promise for versatile material systems due to their distinctive crystalline polymorphism, tunable spontaneous polarization, and diverse molecular relaxation mechanisms1. For ferroelectric polymers, their molecular chains possess abundant internal rotational degrees of freedom. This enables chain segments to undergo various types of internal motions akin to Brownian motion, where each specific internal rotation mode corresponds to a characteristic relaxation time and dipole moment2. In contrast to inorganic materials, whose rigid crystalline lattices inherently constrain the diversity and quantity of intrinsic polarization mechanisms3–5, ferroelectric polymers possess inherently dynamic polarization and relaxation characteristics, making them promising candidates for achieving highly efficient electromagnetic (EM) responses.

Poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) is a representative ferroelectric polymer that has been extensively investigated due to its remarkable polarization properties6–8. The most common α-phase is thermodynamically stable but non-polar, whereas the ferroelectric β-phase, obtained through phase-transition induction strategies, significantly enhances the intrinsic polarization strength and introduces notable dielectric loss behavior. This provides an effective pathway for developing advanced functional materials with multi-band compatibility and efficient electromagnetic energy dissipation. Nevertheless, the practical application of β-phase PVDF still faces several challenges, including low content, poor phase uniformity, and insufficient structural stability9. Owing to the difficulty in precisely controlling polymer chain conformations at the atomic scale, conventional thermal or electrical poling methods tend to cause macroscopic deformation and heterogeneous domain structures in β-PVDF10. This results in reduced ferroelectric phase content, non-uniform distribution, and a consequent significant decline in polarization performance and stability, ultimately impairing device reliability.

In the frontier of scientific fields such as electromagnetics, next-generation communications, and electromagnetic protection, overcoming the technical bottleneck of multi-band efficient EM loss represents a core requirement for addressing complex EM environments11–13. This imposes stricter requirements on the operational stability of ferroelectric PVDF. Effective regulation of PVDF molecular chain conformations at the atomic scale to reduce the system energy of the β-phase below that of the α-phase represents a crucial strategy for enhancing its thermodynamic stability and application potential. Furthermore, the narrow energy difference between the α- and β-phases makes the ferroelectric β-phase susceptible to irreversible transition to the non-ferroelectric α-phase under external disturbances14. This inherent instability significantly limits its applicability under electromagnetic fields. Thus, maintaining a sufficiently large energy difference between the two phases is essential for ensuring structural stability and functional reliability under service conditions.

To fully exploit the effect of PVDF ferroelectric phase on EM wave loss, this study introduces a crystal facet engineering strategy to induce ferroelectric phase transformation within the polymer. Through precisely controlled synthesis to selectively expose the {100} and {111} crystal facets of NiS2, stable and precise control of ferroelectric polymer molecular chains has been achieved at the atomic scale. The mediation of polymer interfaces by specific plane orientations was systematically investigated, elucidating the key microscopic factors through which inorganic fillers influence the stability of the ferroelectric phase of PVDF. This work establishes the crystal facet control of inorganic fillers as a variable for manipulating the ferroelectric phase and molecular dipole distribution in PVDF. Furthermore, the crystal facet-stabilized PVDF matrix significantly enhances the operational stability and reliability of the composite. This study elucidates that ferroelectric polymers exhibit enhanced cross-frequency polarization loss and tunable electromagnetic attenuation, operating from the MHz to GHz range and extending into the THz band. These properties originate from their enhanced polarization intensity along with multiple polarization mechanisms accompanied by a broad distribution of relaxation times. Concurrently, we propose an electromagnetic modulation mechanism based on polarons in highly ferroelectric polymers, enabling multi-band operation, which breaks the trade-off between high loss and wide bandwidth.

---

## Results

PVDF is one of the most researched ferroelectric polymers due to its electroactive properties and ability to form complex structures15,16. Figure S1 shows the most studied and used TGTḠ conformation (T: trans; G: gauche, non-polar α-phase), and the all-trans TTTT conformation (ferroelectric polar β-phase) of PVDF. The presence of an electric dipole moment in the PVDF monomer unit is caused by the larger electronegativity of the fluorine atom, when compared to the neighboring carbon and hydrogen atoms. Therefore, each chain possesses a dipole moment perpendicular to the polymer chain.

Density functional theory (DFT) calculations yielded the crystal structures of the different phases of PVDF with their charge density distributions along the (001) plane. The monomers in the α-phase show a non-polar crystal structure due to the centrosymmetric stacking of their charge density distributions (Fig. S2). The monomers in the β-phase are stacked in a parallel fashion within the unit cell, determining the modulation of the charge density, and resulting in a larger dipole moment (Figs. S3, S4).

Figure 1A demonstrates the polar phase transition mechanism of PVDF on the {100} and {111} crystal facets of NiS2 17. Figure S5 shows the adsorption energies per unit (CH2-CF2) (Ē ads) of α-phase PVDF and β-phase PVDF on the {100} and {111} crystal facets of NiS2. By comparing the interactions of different crystal facets with different phases of PVDF (Fig. S6), it can be observed that the adsorption energies of different PVDFs relative to NiS2 under the same facets ({100} or {111}) differ significantly, which leads to the determination of the dominant conformation of PVDFs on different facets. This provides a theoretical basis for the effect of crystal facet engineering on the phase transition of PVDF.

In Fig. S5A, using DFT calculations, the Ē ads of NiS2 {100} facet with α-phase PVDF is −0.054 eV, while the Ē ads with β-phase PVDF is significantly reduced to −0.186 eV. As seen in Fig. S5B, the Ē ads of NiS2 {111} facet with α-phase PVDF is −0.069 eV, while the Ē ads is slightly reduced to −0.097 eV for β-phase PVDF. This shows that the β-phase of PVDF has a stronger adsorption capacity than the α-phase on the {100} facet, and that the {100} facet is more susceptible to inducing a ferroelectric phase transition in PVDF. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that the all-trans conformation of the β-phase allows for greater polarity and a good complementary contact interface with the NiS2 surface. In this case, the average distance between the S atoms and H atoms in the β-phase is significantly shorter for the {100} facet (2.758 nm) than for the {111} one (2.938 nm). The closer proximity, combined with the coplanar arrangement of S atoms in the {100} facet, results in stronger S-H interactions. Consequently, the β-phase of PVDF demonstrates enhanced adsorption stability when interacting with the NiS2 {100} facet. Compared with the {100} facets, the {111} ones show a relatively small energy difference in the interaction with PVDF (Fig. S6). This result suggests that the variation in energy under different combinations of crystal facets and phases reflects the complexity of material interactions under different environments. The differences in adsorption energies reflect the orientation of the PVDF molecular chains, the distribution of polar centers and their effectiveness in surface interactions.

On the {111} facet, the coordination environment of surface S atoms is near complete saturation, whereas on the {100} facet, both surface Ni and S atoms possess a high density of unsaturated coordination sites, resulting in a higher surface energy (Fig. S7). These unsaturated sites form high-density local polarization centers, making the {100} facet more polar and significantly enhancing interfacial electron coupling and charge transfer capabilities (Figs. S8–S10, Supplementary Tables S1, S2). The higher polarity implies that the {100} facet readily undergoes strong dipole-dipole interactions with β-PVDF molecular chains, which themselves exhibit relatively high surface energy and polarity. This, in turn, makes the {100} facet key to inducing and stabilizing the strongly polar β-phase of PVDF.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations reveal distinct morphological differences in NiS2 particles on different facets. Figure 1B demonstrates that NiS2 particles on the {100} facet exhibit a uniform nanocube (NCs) structure, while Fig. 1D shows that those on the {111} facet adopt an octahedra (OC) morphology. These morphological variations further highlight the differences in crystal structure between the two planes. Additionally, spherical aberration-corrected High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) in Fig. 1C, E reveals differences in the atomic arrangement on both crystal facets. Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) was employed to characterize the composition and spatial distribution of the elements Ni and S (Fig. S11).

A systematic investigation was performed on the crystal structure and electronic states of NiS2 with distinct crystal facets, as well as PVDF/NiS2 (P/N) samples. Figure S12 presents the detailed results of the X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) analysis of NiS2 samples with two main crystal facets, {100} and {111}. The XRD spectra show that the {111} facet exhibits a higher diffraction intensity ratio of the (111) to (200) facets compared to the {100} facet of NiS2. The X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) spectra of elemental Ni and S for the two crystal facets are illustrated in Fig. S13, which show similar features in the high-resolution XPS spectra of Ni and S. The peaks of Ni 2p3/2 and Ni 2p1/2 in the Ni 2p spectra indicate that Nickel is primarily present in the oxidation state (Ⅱ). At 855.8 eV, the secondary spectral peak intensity of the {100} facet of NiS2 exceeds that of the {111} facet, which is attributed to the higher density of undercoordinated Ni sites on the {100} facet18,19. These sites exhibit enhanced susceptibility to oxidation, thus forming higher oxidation states. In addition, the characteristic peaks of the S 2p spectrum reveal that different valence states of sulfur exist on these two crystal facets, suggesting that there is a significant difference in the electronic states of Ni and S on different crystal facets, which originates from the varying surface structure and atomic arrangement20.

The crystal structure of pure PVDF and the P/N samples were analyzed using XRD (Figs. S14, S15) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) characterizations (Fig. S16) to investigate their optical properties. The XRD spectra of P/N samples containing 15 wt.% and 25 wt.% different crystal facets of NiS2 are presented in Fig. 2A, B, respectively. In both compositions, the presence of α and β phases is significant, and the intensity and sharpness of the diffraction peaks vary with increasing NiS2 content. Specifically, the (020) and (110) α-phase diffraction peaks at 18.30° and 19.90° weaken with increasing NiS2 content, while the β-phase (110)/(200) peak at 20.26° intensifies21,22. Moreover, compared to the P/N{111}, the P/N{100} sample exhibits stronger β-phase PVDF diffraction peaks, demonstrating that the {100} facet of NiS2 promotes a higher proportion of ferroelectric β-phase PVDF. The changes in the IR absorption features suggest a shift in the internal molecular structure of the material, which arises from the varying degrees of phase transformation in PVDF. As illustrated in Figs. 2C, D, S17, S18, and Table S3, NiS2 with different crystal facets induces differing ratios of β-phase PVDF, where P/N{100} exhibits a higher β-phase PVDF content. The observed pattern aligns with the conclusions derived from analysis of XRD results. The filler loading (Figs. S19, S20, Supplementary Table S4), shape distributions (Figs. S21–S23, Supplementary Table S5) and filler size (Figs. S24, S25, Supplementary Table S6) were systematically varied. Through comparative analysis, the effects of these macroscopic geometric variables were isolated, thus establishing the specific crystal facet as a core variable in influencing performance.

HRTEM characterizations (Fig. 2E, F) were performed on the P/N samples. PVDF at the nanoparticle/polymer interface exhibits a mixture of TGTḠ and all-trans conformations, which clearly indicates the boundaries of the NiS2 crystal facets and the interactions with the PVDF23. In order to provide direct evidence of the polar phase network induced in the PVDF at different crystal facets, we performed spatial chemical analyses using atomistic-microscopy-based infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) with a laser irradiated at 1280 cm−1 (Fig. 2G–I). Localized IR spectroscopy demonstrates that the addition of NiS2 to PVDF induces the growth of an all-trans conformation (Fig. 2J–L), while no ferroelectric phase is evident in the PVDF spectrum.

In the ferroelectric polymer PVDF, molecular chains with an all-trans conformation stack to form a hexagonal crystal structure (Fig. 3A)17,24. Analysis of the system energy and polarization degree of the PVDF ferroelectric phase during the ferroelectric reversal process was performed using DFT calculations. The results indicate that its polarization response mainly stems from the reorientation of dipoles under the action of an external electric field (Fig. 3B, C). Further analysis of the system energy during the reversal process reveals that the electric field-induced polarization change is achieved through the continuous 60° rotation of dipoles (Fig. S26). It is noteworthy that when the dipoles rotate from 0° to 180°, a significant polarization change occurs, and the lattice strain remains zero during this process2.

To explore the differential induction effect of different crystal facets of NiS2 on the ferroelectric phase of PVDF, piezoelectric force microscopy (PFM) was used to detect the local electrical activity on the surface of P/N samples. In PFM measurements, a conductive probe with higher stiffness (k=20 N/m) was used to suppress long-range electrostatic forces. To eliminate the influence of electrostatic fields on the piezoelectric response, the surface potential was measured via Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) (Fig. S27)25. Subsequently, during PFM testing, a direct-current bias of equal magnitude but of opposite polarity to the measured surface potential was used over the same region to compensate for the surface potential. Figure 3D–G shows the phase (Fig. 3D, F) and amplitude (Fig. 3E, G) hysteresis loops of the PVDF composites induced by different crystal facets. The piezoelectric signal is related to the local polarization switching and ferroelectric properties of P/N samples26. With the increase of voltage, a 180° phase change is observed, and a hysteresis loop is observed during voltage sweep back, which indicates the presence of ferroelectric polarization characteristics in P/N samples. This is direct evidence for the existence of polar polymer crystals and the induction of ferroelectric phase transition in PVDF by crystal facets. In comparison, the coercive voltage of the P/N{100} is 0.68 V, which is lower than that of the P/N{111} (2.85 V). Moreover, the P/N{100} exhibits a larger piezoelectric coefficient with d33=215.31 pm·V−1, indicating that the {100} crystal facet can induce the ferroelectric phase transition of PVDF at a higher efficiency (Figs. S28–S31, Table S7)27. Macroscopic ferroelectric performance tests at room temperature were conducted on pure PVDF, P/N{111}, and P/N{100} samples. The measurement results (as shown in Fig. S32) clearly demonstrate that the P/N{100} exhibits a typical ferroelectric P–E hysteresis loop with well-defined remnant polarization (Pr) and coercive field (Ec). Compared to pure PVDF and P/N{111}, P/N{100} shows significantly higher remnant polarization and saturation polarization (Ps)28. This result directly confirms that the {100} facet not only induces the formation of a local ferroelectric phase in PVDF (as revealed by PFM phase hysteresis) but also enables the composite to exhibit enhanced and switchable ferroelectric polarization at the macroscopic level. Meanwhile, temperature-dependent dielectric measurements demonstrate pronounced relaxor ferroelectric behavior in the P/N{100} (Fig. S33)1,28.

However, despite advances in promoting formation of the β-phase through inorganic doping29–31, existing methodologies struggle to precisely elucidate the regulatory relationship between PVDF phase structure and EM polarization loss performance. The impact of crystal facet engineering on the ferroelectric phase transition of PVDF is evaluated through EM response, where an increase in the β-phase of PVDF content significantly enhances the EM loss capability across various frequency bands. Figure 4A illustrates the complex permittivity (ε‘ and ε“) of PVDF composites with different crystal facets (NiS2 filler loading of 30 wt.%, 40 wt.%, and 50 wt.%) compared to pure PVDF within the frequency range of 0.05 MHz to 100 MHz. Experimental results reveal that the permittivity of pure PVDF is consistently lower than that of P/N samples under the same conditions, consistent with characterization data indicating that hot-pressed PVDF primarily consists of the non-polar α-phase. Further analysis of the frequency-dependent behavior of the imaginary permittivity (ε“) reveals that the ε“ peak for the P/N samples occurs at frequencies below 0.05 MHz. This peak corresponds to a characteristic relaxation process within the P/N samples. According to Debye theory, the relationship between polarization loss and frequency is governed by the relaxation time (τ)32, the observation of this peak below 0.05 MHz directly implies that the corresponding τ exceeds a value of 3.18 μs (Fig. S34). The EM loss capability of the materials can be assessed by the dissipation factor within the 0.05 MHz-100 MHz range31. Figures 4B, S35 and 4C demonstrate that the dissipation factors of both P/N{111} and P/N{100} surpass those of pure PVDF. Due to the varying degrees of interaction between different crystal facets and β-phase PVDF, the dissipation factors of P/N{100} are generally higher than those of P/N{111}. Notably, the maximum dissipation factor of P/N{100}-50% reaches 448.46, significantly higher than that of P/N{111}-50% (322.49). Both sample values, however, are substantially greater than the maximum dissipation factor observed for pure PVDF (0.28). Moreover, the dissipation factors for both samples increase with higher filler loading, a phenomenon attributed to the rise in ferroelectric β-phase PVDF content driven by crystal facet engineering.

The microwave frequency band of 2–18 GHz is widely applicable in various scenarios, particularly in communication, radar, and electronic warfare. To validate the EM loss capabilities resulting from polarization enhancement induced by the PVDF ferroelectric phase transition through crystal facet engineering, microwave absorption performance was selected as a key criterion33. In consideration of impedance matching (MZ), a lower filler loading was chosen for sample testing. Figure 4D illustrates that P/N{100} exhibits higher permittivity compared to P/N{111} at the same filler loading. Within the 2–18 GHz frequency band, the dielectric loss peak of the P/N sample occurs at 6.95 GHz, corresponding to a polarization relaxation process with a relaxation time of 22.91 ps (Fig. S36). To further investigate the root cause of dielectric loss in P/N samples, conduction loss and polarization loss were evaluated separately (Fig. 4E)34. The results indicate that, due to the low conductivity of P/N samples (Figs. S37–S39, Table S8), the dominant loss mechanism in the 2–18 GHz range is polarization loss, which aligns with the trend observed in the imaginary part of the dielectric constant. Additionally, NiS2 with different crystal facets mixed with paraffin exhibits lower and nearly identical dielectric constants, indirectly confirming that the enhancement in dielectric constant originates from the presence of β-phase PVDF (Fig. S40). Based on these findings, it can be concluded that the varying degrees of PVDF phase transition induced by NiS2 with different crystal facets are the primary factor influencing polarization loss in the 2–18 GHz range. The dielectric loss tangent exhibits the same trend. (Figs. 4F, S41). The comparative analysis of the electromagnetic parameters of NiS2 with varying size and shape distributions further underscore the critical role of specific crystal facets in regulating β-PVDF content (Figs. S42, S43).

By evaluating the EM wave absorption performance calculated from the EM parameters of the P/N{100} and P/N{111} with varying filler loadings (Figs. 4G, S44–S46), P/N{100}-20% sample demonstrates optimal performance, achieving a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) value of -62.08 dB and a maximum effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of 4.35 GHz (Fig. S47). Two key factors influencing EM wave absorption capacity analyzed include: impedance matching (MZ) and attenuation constant (α)35. For impedance matching characteristics, the MZ contour plots reveal that the P/N{100}-20% sample exhibits a larger contour in the region where MZ exceeds 0.8 (Fig. 4H), indicating superior impedance matching. Meanwhile, among samples with different crystal facets, the attenuation constants of the P/N{100} are consistently higher than those of the P/N{111} at the same filler loading. Additionally, the attenuation constants of all samples increase with higher filler loading (Figs. 4I, S48), which can be attributed to the increased β-phase PVDF content as the NiS2 filler loading rises, leading to enhanced polarization loss. The attenuation performance of the P/N{100} was systematically compared with state-of-the-art polymer composites reported in recent literature within the 2–18 GHz frequency band. The results demonstrate that the P/N{100} exhibits superior attenuation characteristics across the entire frequency band, outperforming the aforementioned reference systems (Fig. S49)36–41. To further elucidate the unique contribution of the PVDF ferroelectric phase, the attenuation performance of NiS2 composites was also compared with other polymer matrices, as shown in Figs. S50, S51. These results confirm that the formation of the ferroelectric β-phase in PVDF plays a critical role in enhancing electromagnetic wave absorption. The Cole-Cole curve for P/N samples exhibits more pronounced semicircles, indicating the presence of stronger polarization relaxation processes (Fig. S52)41,42. These findings underscore the critical role of crystal facet engineering in optimizing the polar structure of ferroelectric PMs and thereby enhancing microwave absorption properties.

To further evaluate the electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) stealth capability of the P/N samples, radar cross-section (RCS) simulations of perfect electrical conductor (PEC) substrates coated with P/N{100}-20% sample were performed43. The results are presented in the form of three-dimensional RCS intensity images. The major flap reflection signal of the P/N{100}-20% coated PEC substrate is 34.83 dBm2 lower than that of the uncoated PEC substrate, indicating its enhanced EM wave absorption capability (Fig. S53). Figure S53B also shows the simulated RCS values in polar coordinates over the −90 to 90 detection range, highlighting its potential for wide-angle stealth applications. These results indicate that a higher content of PVDF in the β-phase is favorable for enhancing microwave absorption, while different degrees of the ferroelectric phase transition in PVDF can be induced by different crystal facets.

The terahertz band, as a key frequency range for the sixth generation of mobile communication, operates at higher frequencies and energies, making the study of EM wave loss in this band particularly important44. Terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) was conducted in transmission mode to evaluate the properties of P/N sample films (Fig. 5A)45. Compared to the air reference, the terahertz signal experiences significant attenuation when passing through the P/N sample films (Fig. 5B–D). Shielding performance and transmittance were used to assess the EM properties of these films in the 0.2–2.0 THz range46. The results show that the terahertz shielding performance of P/N{111} films is lower than that of P/N{100} at the same filler loading, further confirming that the presence of PVDF in the β-phase enhances the terahertz shielding performance (Figs. S54, S55). For the total terahertz shielding effectiveness (SET) at a low thickness of 0.25 mm, P/N{100}-50% sample demonstrates the best performance with a maximum value of 29.91 dB (shielding efficiency (α SE) of 99.90%), an average value of 21.91 dB, and a minimum value higher than 10 dB (Figs. 5E, F, S56). Through the measurement and calculation of the reflection and multiple reflection components within regions of effective shielding, it is determined that the shielding performance of P/N{100}-50% is primarily attributed to absorption loss, while the contributions from multiple reflections and scattering are negligible (Figs. S57–S59)47–49.

Further analysis indicates a statistically significant linear positive correlation between β-phase content and terahertz shielding effectiveness (Figs. S60, S61). The established regression model (Table S9, Fig. S62) exhibits excellent goodness-of-fit (R2=0.94442) and high statistical significance (p=0.00738), providing robust quantitative evidence that β-phase content is a key determinant of terahertz attenuation performance. This statistically confirms that as the β-phase content in the sample increases systematically, its terahertz shielding effectiveness demonstrates a linear growth trend. This outcome is entirely consistent with our proposed theoretical mechanism: a higher proportion of β-phase PVDF results in stronger dipole and interfacial polarization, which are primary factors of terahertz wave energy dissipation. The transmittance of the two materials aligns with their shielding performance trends (Figs. 5G, H, S63). The minimum transmittance of the P/N{100}-50% sample is 0.032, with an average of 0.090; both values are higher than those of the other P/N samples.

The extinction coefficients of P/N-50% samples were calculated from the frequency domain spectra (Fig. S64). This enables the derivation of ε“ (Fig. 5I) and the absorption coefficients (αT) (Fig. 5J). Here, ε“ elucidates THz-band relaxation dynamics, whereas αT serves as a metric for terahertz EM wave attenuation50. The ε“ of the P/N samples exhibits a distinct peak at 0.3 THz, corresponding to a relaxation process in the THz band with a relaxation time of 0.53 ps. This process coexists with multiple secondary relaxation modes across the terahertz spectrum. The P/N samples show higher absorption coefficients compared to pure PVDF, and the αT of the P/N{111} is lower than that of the P/N{100}. This suggests that the presence of the β-phase in PVDF increases EM loss in the THz band. This confirms that the crystal facet-mediated ferroelectric polarity in PVDF drives polarization response mechanisms in the THz spectrum.

Polarization mechanisms are the core for regulating the EM response of P/N ferroelectric samples. Benefiting from their abundant molecular chain rotational freedom and spontaneous polarization characteristics, organic ferroelectric polymers can leverage intrinsic multi-relaxation mechanisms to reconfigure the distribution of extreme values in electromagnetic parameters. This broadens the relaxation time, thus facilitating highly efficient broadband electromagnetic energy response51. In multi-band EM loss, it plays a crucial role through the synergistic effects of interfacial, spatial, and orientational dipole polarizations. The functions of each polarization mechanism in different frequency bands are as follows: As shown in Fig. S65, in the MHz frequency band, the loss mode of P/N ferroelectric samples is dominated by interfacial dipole polarization loss. The difference in permittivity between the ferroelectric phase PVDF and the inorganic filler induces interfacial dipoles. Under the action of an external EM field, these interfacial dipoles undergo rotational polarization. Through the dipole relaxation process, the EM energy in the MHz frequency band is converted into heat energy and dissipated, achieving EM loss in this frequency band52. When entering the GHz frequency band, the polar groups of the ferroelectric phase PVDF are affected by EM fluctuations, resulting in changes in dipole moment in the spatial dimension. The spatial distribution state of molecular chains directly affects the polarization efficiency, enabling targeted dissipation capability for EM waves in the GHz frequency band. At this time, the dipoles dissipate the EM waves in the GHz frequency band through vibration and rotation53.

As the frequency increases, the orientational rotation of dipoles in the alternating EM field becomes increasingly intense. In the THz frequency band, since the ferroelectric phase PVDF is a semi-crystalline polymer, the synergistic effect of the crystalline and amorphous phase structures in the sample promotes the orientational adjustment of dipole molecules under the THz high-frequency EM field (Fig. S66). Factors such as the characteristics of the crystal-amorphous interface and the degree of molecular chain orientation determine the polarization relaxation characteristics, which can precisely match the EM loss requirements in the THz frequency band, and realize energy dissipation through the orientational adjustment process of dipoles54. In summary, P/N ferroelectric samples utilize the synergy of interfacial, spatial, and orientational dipole polarizations. Different polarization mechanisms jointly regulate the EM response of the material across multiple frequency bands to achieve multi-band EM loss (Fig. S67).

Compared to ferroelectric EM loss materials reported in recent studies, the P/N samples proposed in this work maintain superior loss capability across various frequency bands. The evaluation metrics for material performance vary with electromagnetic frequency bands: in the MHz band, it is determined by the dissipation factor; in the GHz band, it is based on effective bandwidth and reflection loss; and in the THz band, the shielding effectiveness per unit thickness is employed (Fig. S68, Table S10)50,55–68. This performance stems from the diverse polarization types generated by the ferroelectric phase transition of PVDF and the broad distribution of relaxation times in PM samples. These provide valuable insights for developing advanced broadband EM compatibility materials.

In summary, this study demonstrates a facet-induced strategy for modulation of stable and uniform polymer ferroelectric phase, revealing the pivotal regulatory role of intrinsic polarization properties in the ferroelectric polymer matrix for governing multi-band efficient electromagnetic responses. By the combination of first-principle calculations and AFM experimental procedures, it is demonstrated that the {100} crystal facet of NiS2 stabilizes the ferroelectric β-phase PVDF by reducing its energy below that of the non-ferroelectric phase and increasing its energy difference, thereby achieving a stabilized ferroelectric PVDF system and multi-band EM dissipation performance. This effect arises from the spontaneous polarization induced by the ferroelectric phase β-PVDF, leading to a broad distribution of relaxation times and enhancing multiple types of polarization mechanisms, with relaxation frequencies across megahertz, gigahertz, and terahertz frequency ranges. As a direct manifestation of these phenomena, enhanced polarization loss and a systematic increase in absorption coefficient are observed. These findings not only elucidate the mechanism of crystal facet engineering-driven PVDF ferroelectric phase transition evolution but also establish a synergistic principle linking the ferroelectric polarization of organic PM, multi-band frequency response expansion, and enhanced EM wave loss.

## Methods

Preparation of NiS2 nanocrystals with {111}-exposed surfaces: 0.20 mmol NiCl2·6H2O, 0.50 mmol Na2S2O3·5H2O, and 0.165 g of PVP with MW∼58,000 were dissolved in 76 ml deionized water, and then stirred for 30 min at room temperature and normal pressure to make the solution well mixed and homogeneous, and then placed in a 100 ml hydrothermal reactor. The reaction was carried out in a 100 ml hydrothermal reactor at 150 °C for 12 h, and then naturally cooled to room temperature. The obtained product was centrifuged several times with deionized water and anhydrous ethanol, and the black precipitate was taken and dried in an oven to obtain NiS2 nanocrystals with {111} exposed surfaces, which were named as NiS2{111}.

Preparation of NiS2 nanocrystals with {100} exposed faces: 2.40 mmol of Ni(NO3)2·6H2O, 10.00 mmol of C2H4N2S, 0.65 g of Mw~58000 PVP and 0.05 mmol of NaOH were dissolved in 40 ml of deionized water, and then stirred for 30 min at room temperature and pressure to make the solution fully mixed and homogeneous, and then placed in a 100 ml hydrothermal reactor. The reaction was carried out in a 100 ml hydrothermal reactor at 150 °C for 12 h, and then naturally cooled to room temperature. The obtained product was centrifuged several times repeatedly with deionized water and anhydrous ethanol, and the black precipitate was taken and dried in an oven to obtain NiS2 nanocrystals with {100} exposed surfaces, which were named as NiS2{100}.

Preparation of NiS2/PVDF samples: NiS2 nanocrystals with {100} and {111} exposed surfaces were mixed with pure PVDF at different mass fillings, dissolved and dispersed in DMF, and dried at 80 °C to form a thin film. The films were hot-pressed at 220 °C and 5 MPa for 20 min and then cooled naturally to form NiS2/PVDF cylindrical-shaped samples (Φ out=7.00 mm and Φ in=3.04 mm). NiS2/PVDF sample films were pressed to a thickness of 0.25 mm using the same temperature and pressure. NiS2/PVDF samples are named P/N{hkl}-X, where {hkl} is the crystal facet of NiS2 and X is the filler loading of NiS2.

Material characterizations: The morphology of the resulting nanoparticles was studied by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Quanta 250 FEG) and scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM, Thermofisher Spectra 300). The elemental composition and spatial distribution were characterized via energy dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS, Super X EDS detector). The crystal structure of the nanostructures was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) on a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer equipped with a copper target at a wavelength of 1.5418 Å. The elemental composition was characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (Thermo Scientific K-Alpha). The U-I curves of the samples were measured by a semiconductor analyzer (Keithley 2400). AFM-IR measurements were carried out on a Bruker Anasys nanoIR3 system. Both topography and chemical images were simultaneously collected in the tapping mode. The local IR spectra were obtained by placing the atomic force microscope tip on top of the sample. The HRTEM images were captured on FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The film was precisely sectioned using a Leica EM UC7 ultramicrotome. After that, the sectioned samples were placed on the copper carrier network support carbon film for transmission electron microscopy imaging. Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) and Piezoelectric reaction force microscopy (PFM) were performed on a commercial atomic force microscope (OXFORD-MFP-3D Origin+). High-stiffness conductive probes (k≈20 N/m) were used in the experiments. To obtain a local piezoelectric response loop, the DC switch is switched from −30 V to 30 V. The ferroelectric P-E hysteresis loops were measured using a Radiant Precision LC II tester (USA). The temperature-dependent dielectric constant was measured using an Agilent 4294A impedance analyzer (USA) over a temperature range of 20 °C to 150 °C at frequencies of 10 kHz, 100 kHz, 1 MHz, and 2 MHz.

DFT calculations: The DFT calculations were performed using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP) in the projected augmented wave framework. The generalized gradient approximation proposed by Perdew, Burke and Ernzerhof (PBE) was chosen for the exchange-correlation potential. The energy cutoff of the plane wave was set to 550 eV. We used k-point grids of 10×6×3 for PVDF, 2×2×1 for NiS2, and 1×1×1 for NiS2/PVDF. The convergence criteria for geometry optimizations were a maximum residual force of less than 0.05 V·Å−1 and an energy change of less than 10−5 eV.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript reports a facet-engineering approach using NiS₂ crystal planes ({100} and {111}) to stabilize the β-phase of PVDF, achieving broadband electromagnetic (EM) loss from MHz to THz. The authors combine DFT calculations, structural characterizations (SEM, TEM, XRD, FTIR, AFM-IR, PFM), and EM response analysis to demonstrate that facet modulation enables enhanced polarization and relaxation dynamics, breaking the Kramers–Kronig trade-off. The topic is original, the data are extensive, and the idea of facet-modulated ferroelectricity in polymers is both novel and technologically relevant. However, several methodological, mechanistic, and presentation aspects require significant improvement before acceptance.
1. The manuscript claims that {100} facets of NiS₂ stabilize β-PVDF by lowering its energy below α-PVDF. However, the underlying electronic or interfacial mechanism is insufficiently elaborated.
2. How does charge transfer or dipole alignment differ quantitatively between facets?
3. Can authors provide charge density difference maps or Bader charge analysis to support the interfacial polarization claims?
4. The statement that this mechanism “breaks the Kramers–Kronig constraint” seems physically overstated, since these relations are fundamental. The authors should instead clarify that multi-relaxation mechanisms mitigate the apparent loss–bandwidth trade-off.
5. Is there any specific cause of choosing NiS2 as the filler material?
6. Provide the investigation of a control composite with randomly oriented NiS₂ or another inert filler to confirm that the observed effects are truly facet-specific.
7. The role of NiS₂ conductivity in EM attenuation must be disentangled from ferroelectric polarization effects (conductivity data in Table S1 suggest notable variation).
8. The PFM data (Fig. 3D–G) show phase hysteresis, but there is no macroscopic polarization–electric field (P–E) loop. A P–E measurement or Sawyer–Tower loop is essential to confirm bulk ferroelectricity.
9. The reported coercive voltages (0.41 V and 0.62 V) are relatively low. Clarify whether these values refer to local switching or macroscopic measurement.
10. Table S2 shows strong EM loss compared to other materials, but normalization (per thickness, per filler loading, etc.) is inconsistent.
11. Please include a clear benchmark plot (e.g., attenuation constant vs. frequency) comparing state-of-the-art polymer composites.
12. The claim that the system “overcomes the limitation imposed by Kramers–Kronig relations” is conceptually problematic. These relations are not breakable for causal, linear systems. The authors could instead argue that nonlinear ferroelectric polarization and multi-relaxation processes expand the effective response bandwidth.
13. The reported THz shielding effectiveness (≈30 dB for 0.25 mm) is impressive but could also arise from multiple reflection and scattering effects. Consider adding complex refractive index or impedance spectra to clarify this.
14. The correlation between β-phase fraction and THz attenuation should be statistically supported (e.g., regression of β-phase ratio vs. SET).
15. The SEM/TEM images (Fig. 1B–E) show morphological differences, but facet indexing and atomic models should be more explicitly correlated.
16. A surface energy or coordination number comparison would reinforce the claim that {100} facets are more polarizing.
17. The Introduction could better emphasize how this work differs from previous PVDF–inorganic interface engineering (e.g., doped or hybridized PVDF systems).

### Reviewer 2

Facet-Modulated Ferroelectric Polymers-Major comments to the authors:
The present work tried to correlate the effect of facets of the crystal on the PVDF structure and its properties is a novel idea for research, however, the approach the authors followed requires further improvements with following suggestions/modifications/required new experiments.
1. The individual crystal facet implication on the β-phase of PVDF has been elaborated, however, the quantitative analysis of increase in β-phase as a function of particle size distribution and shape distribution is required as the physical properties measured are average properties of over the area of the samples. Hence it is desired to understand the shape and size distributions and their effect on β-phase is required.
2. A clear comparison between the PFM results for pure PVDF and composite is required. The effect of enhancement of β-phase on the PFM related physical quantities must be emphasized. The piezoelectric tensor matrix analysis for the pure and composites has to be incorporated with respect to observed PFM results.
3. However, the butterfly loop is not fully saturated, the reason and a comparison with earlier literature need to be incorporated.
4. The title “Facet-Modulated Ferroelectric Polymers” showcases the ferroelectric nature of the composite, however the ferroelectric properties such as Polarization versus Electric field and Analysis of Curie’s Temperature from temperature dependent dielectric properties has not been incorporated. The authors are strongly suggested to incorporate the same for further consideration.
With the above suggestions, the manuscript is not suggested for publication in nature communications in the present form, however if the authors would like to add the above measurements/provide the appropriate data, the manuscript may be reconsidered after thorough revision.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript by B. Cai et al. reports a method for preferential crystallization of the ferroelectric β-phase of PVDF on specific facets of NiS2 nanocrystals. The authors attribute this effect to enhanced S-H interactions at the {100} surface. However, the experimental data do not convincingly support this conclusion, and several key interpretations are either incomplete or unsupported.
1. The XRD diffractograms (Figs. 2A,B and S11) show a dominant β-phase peak in all sample, while the differences in FTIR spectra are minimal and even disappears at 25% NiS2 loading (Figs. 2C,D and S12). These variations fall within the usual batch-to-batch variability of PVDF and cannot be taken as solid evidence of facet-induced β-phase enhancement.
2. A more fundamental issue is that the influence of processing conditions is barely addressed. It is well known that mechanical stretching and elevated temperatures promote α- to β-phase transition in PVDF [https://doi.org/10.1039/C3RA45134H]. The hot-pressing method used by the authors can itself induce β-phase formation, with nanoparticles acting as stress concentrators. A similar effect has already been reported for PVDF-BaTiO3 system [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymertesting.2024.108516]. The authors fail to decouple the contribution of thermal–mechanical processing from any alleged facet-specific effects.
3. The characterization of the PVDF/NiS2 composites physical properties also raises concerns. The PFM data are not convincing. V-shape amplitude loops such of those in Figs. 3E,G are typical of electrostatic artefacts caused by tip-sample interaction, not of genuine piezoresponse [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ultramic.2019.112839]. For samples dominated by non-polar α-phase, the authors should have used stiffer AFM probes, controlled surface potential via KPFM, and performed PFM in both contact and non-contact modes to verify that the response is truly piezoelectric rather than electrostatic.
4. The dielectric measurements are also problematic. The authors conclude (lines 253-254) that “…due to the low conductivity of P/N composites (Figure S17, Table S1), the dominant loss mechanism in the 2-18 GHz range is polarization loss…”. This is contradicted by their own data. Table S1 shows a 4-orders-of-magnitude (!) conductivity increase in P/N{100}, when NiS2 loading increases from 15% to 25%. Such a dramatic change should strongly influence conductive losses, yet Fig. 4E shows no effect at all. This discrepancy is ignored, making further discussion of the electromagnetic properties unreliable.
5. The novelty of the “facet engineering” approach proposed by the authors is overstated. Surface-induced polymorphism in both organic and inorganic systems is well established in literature [https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.201503169; https://doi.org/10.1039/C8CS00283E]. β-phase enhancement in PVDF composites with inorganic nanoparticles has already been demonstrated [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymertesting.2024.108516]. The work does not introduce a sufficiently new concept or mechanism.
In summary, the “facet engineering” concept presented here is not novel, and β-phase enhancement in PVDF-nanoparticle composites has already been demonstrated. The experimental evidence is weak, key controls are missing, and several interpretations are questionable or unsupported. Overall, the originality and scientific rigor of the work do not meet the standards of Nature Communications, and the manuscript should not be accepted for publication.

Q5: Is there any specific cause of choosing NiS as the filler material?
2
material is based on a comprehensive evaluation of crystal plane control, material
stability, electromagnetic properties, and economic and environmental sustainability.
The specific reasons are as follows:
1. Feasibility of Crystal Plane Control: Our research focuses on optimizing the
ferroelectric phase transition of materials by controlling the exposed crystal planes.
NiS can be synthesized via facile methods such as hydrothermal synthesis to
2
effectively control its macroscopic morphology. This enables selective exposure of
specific crystal planes featuring highly ordered and stable atomic arrangements,
providing an ideal model for investigating the interaction mechanisms between crystal
planes and ferroelectric polymers (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed., 2019, 131, 18849-18855).
2. The Comprehensive Advantages of Nickel-Based Materials: We prioritize
nickel-based materials for the following reasons: High Stability: Compared to iron-
based and cobalt-based materials, nickel sulfides exhibit superior stability in air and are
less prone to oxidation. This ensures long-term effectiveness during material
preparation and application. Simultaneously, NiS eliminates magnetic interference: As
2
demonstrated by our electromagnetic parameter testing (Figure S44), NiS exhibits a
2
9
real magnetic permeability (μ') close to 1 and an imaginary permeability (μ'') near 0,
indicating negligible magnetic properties. This eliminates magnetic losses from
contributing to absorptive performance, enabling a purer investigation of dielectric
polarization (including crystal-plane-induced interfacial polarization and dipole
polarization) in electromagnetic wave attenuation.
3. Economic and Environmental Considerations: Nickel is abundant in the
Earth's crust, relatively inexpensive, and its compounds exhibit low environmental
toxicity, aligning with the requirements for sustainable material development.
In summary, NiS combines stable, tunable crystal planes, excellent chemical
2
stability, distinct nonmagnetic properties, economic and environmental advantages,
aligning perfectly with the design objectives of our study. Consequently, it was selected
as the ideal filler material.

differences in testing methods, evaluating the loss characteristics of materials across

evaluation lies in assessing its “ultimate loss potential”—specifically, the strongest
reflection loss and the broadest absorption bandwidth achievable at a given thickness.

Q16: A surface energy or coordination number comparison would reinforce the claim
that {100} facets are more polarizing.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. Using first-principles
calculations, we quantitatively compared the surface energies of different NiS₂ facets.
The results show that the surface energy of the {100} facet (0.1460 eV/Å2) is higher
than that of the {111} facet (0.1219 eV/Å2). This difference stems directly from their
atomic structures: on the {111} facet, the coordination environment of surface S atoms
is nearly saturated, whereas on the {100} facet, both surface Ni and S atoms possess a
high density of unsaturated coordination sites (e.g., vacant orbitals on Ni2+ and lone-
pair electron sites on S 2-), leading to higher surface energy. These unsaturated sites
2
create a high density of local polarization centers, endowing the {100} facet with
32
stronger polarity, which significantly enhances interfacial electron coupling and charge
transfer capability (as confirmed by charge density difference analysis) (Figure R2).
The higher polarity implies that the highly polar {100} facet more readily engages
in strong dipole-dipole interactions with β-PVDF molecular chains, which also exhibit
relatively high surface energy and polarity, thereby serving as the key to inducing and
stabilizing the strongly polar β-phase of PVDF. Therefore, the higher surface energy
and more unsaturated coordination environment together constitute the fundamental
physicochemical reason why the {100} facet possesses stronger polarizing capability
compared to the {111} facet.

This study breaks through the conventional paradigm of regulating PVDF
performance by altering filler “type”, and pioneers the introduction of “crystal facet
engineering” into this system. Instead of merely selecting different inorganic fillers, we
achieve precise and controllable modulation at the atomic scale by accurately
controlling the exposure of specific crystal facets ({100} vs. {111}). We systematically
investigate how specific plane orientations mediate differential interactions of polymer
chains at the interface, elucidating the key microscopic factors through which inorganic
fillers influence the stability of the ferroelectric phase in PVDF. This work establishes
crystal facet control of inorganic fillers as a new variable for manipulating the
ferroelectric phase and molecular dipole distribution in PVDF. It reveals that, due to
differences in atomic arrangement and electronic structure, different crystal facets
36
exhibit fundamentally distinct interfacial interactions with PVDF molecular chains.
This deepens the understanding from a generalized “surface effect” to a microscopic
mechanism based on adsorption energy, surface energy, and charge transfer. Ultimately,
this strategy not only effectively enhances the β-phase content but also synergistically
optimizes its thermodynamic stability and dielectric/ferroelectric activity. It represents
an advancement in the structure-property relationship from merely pursuing content to
the co-design of quality and function, providing a rational and controllable new
paradigm for developing high-performance ferroelectric polymer-based
electromagnetic functional materials.
We have incorporated the comparative analysis and discussion above into the
Introduction and Discussion sections of the revised manuscript. We believe this will
allow the unique contributions and innovative value of this work relative to existing
research to be presented more accurately and convincingly.

Q3: However, the butterfly loop is not fully saturated, the reason and a comparison
with earlier literature need to be incorporated.
Reply: Thank you to the reviewer for their keen observation. This phenomenon is
relatively common in conductive filler/ferroelectric polymer sample systems. The main
reason for the unsaturated loops lies in the leakage current generated by the sample
under high-voltage testing due to the introduction of conductive NiS fillers. This
2
leakage current superimposes on the intrinsic polarization signal from ferroelectric
domain switching, preventing the loops from achieving full saturation and resulting in
the observed slender shape (Ceram. Int., 2021, 47, 23659-23664). This phenomenon
has also been reported in similar conductive filler/ferroelectric polymer systems (such
as graphene/PVDF composites (J. Mater. Chem. A, 2023, 11, 4280-4291)) and
represents a common challenge in the study of such materials.
We note that similar non-saturated P-E loops have been repeatedly reported in
related studies on ferroelectric composites (Adv. Mater., 2021, 33, 2106308, J. Mater.
Chem. A, 2023, 11, 4280-4291, Nat. Commun., 2024, 15, 4702, Nat. Commun., 2025,
16, 3071). The phenomenon of filler-induced leakage currents leading to loop non-
48
saturation is observed in such material systems. Therefore, the behavior observed in our
study aligns with the general physical mechanism common to this class of materials.
Although the incomplete saturation of the loops may affect the absolute accuracy
of the ferroelectric parameters, all samples were prepared and measured under identical
testing conditions. Therefore, these data remain effective for comparing the relative
differences in ferroelectric performance among different samples (e.g., P/N{100} vs.
P/N{111}).
To address this comment, we have supplemented the results in Supplementary
Table S7 and revised the relevant statements in the revised supporting information
accordingly.

spectroscopy piezoresponse force microscopy (SS-PFM) imaging provides direct
evidence of ferroelectric polarization switching behavior. Together, this new
experimental evidence indicates that the signals we observed originate from genuine
piezoelectric/ferroelectric responses, rather than electrostatic artifacts.

Reply: Thank you for the questions raised by the reviewers. We would like to clarify
that there is no contradiction between the experimental data and the conclusions.
Although changes in electrical conductivity do contribute to conductive loss, such loss
constitutes only a minor portion of the overall dielectric loss within the 2-18 GHz
frequency range. Therefore, we maintain that polarization loss remains the dominant
loss mechanism in this frequency band.
Difference in electrical conductivity primarily stems from the distinct geometric
packing characteristics of cubic and octahedral particles. Cubic particles can achieve
dense packing more easily through face-to-face or face-edge contacts, resulting in a
larger effective contact area between particles, which facilitates the formation of
conductive pathways. In contrast, octahedral particles, with their numerous vertices and
edges, tend to form point-to-point or line-to-point contacts during packing. This often
leads to the creation of arch-like structures and voids between particles, thereby
reducing the efficiency of constructing conductive pathways. Consequently, as the filler
content increases, the cubic particle system more readily forms an efficient percolation
network through dense packing, leading to a more pronounced rise in electrical
conductivity (Nature, 2009, 460, 876–879).

Q5: The novelty of the “facet engineering” approach proposed by the authors is
overstated. Surface-induced polymorphism in both organic and inorganic systems is
well established in literature
[https://doi.org/10.1002/adfm.201503169; https://doi.org/10.1039/C8CS00283E]. β-
phase enhancement in PVDF composites with inorganic nanoparticles has already been
demonstrated [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymertesting.2024.108516]. The work does
not introduce a sufficiently new concept or mechanism.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We have carefully studied the
referenced literature cited and would like to provide a clearer elaboration on the novelty
of our work based on this foundation.
Surface/interface effects have been widely demonstrated to regulate the crystalline
morphology of polymers. We note that strategies such as inorganic/organic composites
or nanoparticle composites can effectively influence the phase transitions of polymers
like PVDF. Building upon this foundation, our study further proposes that
systematically designing specific crystal facets can significantly enhance and maximize
such interfacial interactions. Our work represents the first systematic application of
crystallographic facet engineering to ferroelectric polymer systems, establishing an
effective link from atomic-scale interface modulation to macroscopic multi-frequency
electromagnetic responses. This approach not only deepens the understanding of the
regulatory mechanisms behind polymer polymorphism but also provides a transferable
pathway for optimizing interfacial effects in other material systems through facet
engineering.
This study breaks through the conventional paradigm of regulating PVDF
performance by altering filler “type”, and pioneers the introduction of “crystal facet
engineering” into this system. Instead of merely selecting different inorganic fillers, we
achieve precise and controllable modulation at the atomic scale by accurately
controlling the exposure of specific crystal facets ({100} vs. {111}). We systematically
investigate how specific plane orientations mediate differential interactions of polymer
chains at the interface, elucidating the key microscopic factors through which inorganic
fillers influence the stability of the ferroelectric phase in PVDF. This work establishes
crystal facet control of inorganic fillers as a new variable for manipulating the
ferroelectric phase and molecular dipole distribution in PVDF. It reveals that, due to
differences in atomic arrangement and electronic structure, different crystal facets
72
exhibit fundamentally distinct interfacial interactions with PVDF molecular chains.
This deepens the understanding from a generalized “surface effect” to a microscopic
mechanism based on adsorption energy, surface energy, and charge transfer. Ultimately,
this strategy not only effectively enhances the β-phase content but also synergistically
optimizes its thermodynamic stability and dielectric/ferroelectric activity. It represents
an advancement in the structure-property relationship from merely pursuing content to
the co-design of quality and function, providing a rational and controllable new
paradigm for developing high-performance ferroelectric polymer-based
electromagnetic functional materials (Table R11).
